sections.html:
Bordering North Carolina, York County sits in the upper middle of South Carolina and measures about 696 square miles. It is part of the Charlotte metro area, bounded by the Broad River on the west and the Catawba on the east. York, incorporated as Yorkville in 1841, is the county seat, and Rock Hill is the largest city. Tega Cay, Clover, Fort Mill, McConnells, Sharon, Lake Wylie, Hickory Grove and Smyrna fill out the map.

Few counties here have grown faster. Between 2010 and 2020 the population climbed 24.8 percent to 282,090, and the 2025 estimate stands at 306,887. Century-old houses sit beside new subdivisions, which is why your own parcel's value should come from the assessor and not from a county average.

sections.h2: When York County taxes are due
sections.html:
The payment window opens September 30 and stays penalty-free through the following January 15. One notice is printed for each parcel, addressed to the person who held title on January 1. Installments are off the table, since state law doesn't authorize them, which means co-owners have to settle between themselves how to cover the single bill. Lenders can get their own copy by asking the county in writing.

Once January 15 passes, penalties follow S.C. Code 12-45-180. The tax collector can quote an exact payoff, so rely on that rather than doing the arithmetic.

A penalty gets forgiven only if there is direct proof the county made a mistake, for instance one linked to a change of ownership.

sections.h2: Tax notices after you buy or sell
sections.html: A buyer's first bill may show the seller's name, since January 1 ownership controls. The county reassigns it to the new owner a year later. During a year of transfer, your closing attorney should decide how the notice is handled. Tax is normally split between buyer and seller at the closing table, and the attorney can show who owes what.

sections.h2: The 4 percent and 6 percent assessment rates
sections.html:
Your primary home can qualify for a 4 percent assessment, while other residential and commercial property sits at 6 percent. Finding 6 percent on a house you live in? Phone the Tax Assessor, 803-684-8526, and file the legal residence application for 4 percent.

After approval, the auditor sends a fresh notice and cancels the 6 percent one. Where a mortgage company paid the higher figure, the county refunds the difference to it, though processing may take several weeks.

Reappraisal comes every five years under state law. Someone who moved out and now rents the place should plan on the 6 percent rate.

Call the assessor first. Errors such as wrong acreage or a missing 4 percent status often get corrected with no formal appeal. When a call doesn't solve it, send a written objection to the assessor no later than 90 days after the notice was mailed.

From there, each stage runs on a 30 day clock:

  • A written protest following your conference with the assessor.
  • An appeal to the county board of assessment appeals, measured from the assessor's reply.
  • A request for a hearing before the state Administrative Law Court, measured from the board's written decision.

Each October or November the county holds its tax sale. Notices for delinquent real estate run in The Herald weekly for three weeks beforehand, and the county's website carries the date well in advance.

A year of redemption rights follows the sale for the owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor. Redeeming costs the bid plus 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent interest, set by quarter. Certified mail goes out between 20 and 45 days before the year ends.

York County has no countywide water and sewer system. Service comes from the town or private utility serving the street, and a final bill plus a transfer of service is part of most closings. Learn which provider covers your street early.

sections.h2: What to ask before you list
sections.html:
Start with three questions. Is my home at the right rate? Is there any unpaid tax, and what would the payoff be today? Which utility serves the house? Answers to those take a few calls and prevent most closing-week surprises.

If you are selling a house you inherited or one you rent out, add a fourth: who is on the title, and does everyone agree to sell? The closing attorney will need that settled before the deed is drafted. Bring the January 1 ownership facts, your tax notice and any mortgage statement to the first meeting, and keep copies of what you submit to the county.

A cash sale can suit an owner with deferred repairs or a pending tax sale, because it doesn't depend on a buyer's mortgage approval or an appraisal. You compare the written offer with what a listing might net after repairs, carrying costs and the wait, then choose. Either way, the payoff is cleared at closing and the deed is recorded, which finishes the process. Keep the payoff letter, the signed deed and the recording receipt together in one folder afterward, in case a question about the tax year comes up later, whether from a buyer, a lender or the county itself. A tidy paper trail also speeds up any later question about who paid what. Take your time with the numbers, because a sale can't be reversed once the deed is signed.

Deeds carry a $1.85 charge per $500 of value, normally paid by the seller, with $0.55 of it going to the county. Attach an affidavit of value or a statement of why the deed is exempt.

Your attorney drafts the deed and affidavit, orders the payoff and handles the notice question above.

Owing tax doesn't prevent a closing; the balance comes from your proceeds. A typical order of work looks like this.

  • Get a written payoff from the tax collector, with its expiration date.
  • Look for a 6 percent rate that ought to be 4.
  • When a sale date is near, say so to the attorney on day one.
  • Inside a town or city, confirm which utility accounts to close.

faqs.q: When are York County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Payment opens September 30 and is penalty-free until January 15. Whoever owned the property on January 1 is the one billed.

faqs.q: Does York County accept partial property tax payments?
faqs.a: No. State law doesn't allow partial payments, and each parcel gets a single notice, so co-owners must decide together how to pay it.

faqs.q: How do I get the 4 percent assessment in York County?
faqs.a: Phone the Tax Assessor at 803-684-8526 and file the legal residence application. Once approved, a new notice replaces the 6 percent one.

faqs.q: When is the York County tax sale?
faqs.a: Every October or November. The date appears on the county website ahead of time, and The Herald runs the property list weekly for three weeks beforehand.

faqs.q: Why did I get a tax bill after buying a house in York County?
faqs.a: Bills go to the January 1 owner of record, so your first one may show the seller's name. Your closing attorney can explain how the tax was prorated.
